1.why: The reset token is accepted as a bearer value without any association to the requesting email or user.

2.why: A valid unused token can be used by any session because there is no user binding, although the used flag prevents reuse.

3.why: Password reset does not invalidate existing sessions; sessions remain until their time expiry.

4.why: Bun.serve is configured with TLS certificates and HTTP redirects to HTTPS, but the code does not show or pin the latest TLS version.

5.why: TLS protects transit and passwords are Argon2id hashed, but reset tokens are stored in plaintext in memory and no user-data encryption is shown.

6.why: No real email message is implemented, and the simulated delivery exposes the reset token in the page log and console.

7.why: The server enforces strict length and format validation on inputs and the UI writes messages via textContent, but there is no general HTML sanitization routine.

8.why: The only redirect is to a fixed https://localhost origin, but the code does not demonstrate that this host is the hospital’s site.

9.why: No email templating or sending functionality is present, so no user-controlled HTML or script in email content is observable.

10.why: Generic error responses are used, but the client-side logs explicitly print the reset token and MFA code.

11.why: Passwords are Argon2id hashed, but the MFA code is hardcoded in the source and reset tokens are kept in plaintext.

12.why: The fixed MFA code 482916 in the source acts as a default secret that is accepted by the MFA step.

13.why: Token verification and MFA attempts are rate-limited or blocked after repeated failures, but the password-reset endpoint itself lacks a separate wrong-attempt lockout.

14.why: The recovery endpoint returns the same generic message regardless of whether the email is registered and performs no account lookup.

15.why: The reset token is random and long, but it is not bound to a specific user.
